summary: This standards-track document defines new SDP media-level attributes so that when interactive communication sessions are set up, participants can negotiate human language needs. These include spoken, written and signed languages. It lets a call be matched to the languages and modes the people involved can use.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 8373 adds two attributes to the Session Description Protocol so that the people in a call can agree on the language they will use. An offer lists the languages the caller can use, most preferred first. The answer picks one. The attributes are set per direction and per media stream, so a call can use spoken language one way and written language the other.

subtitle: How a caller and a called party agree on spoken, written or signed language while a call is being set up.

tldr.problem: When someone starts a call, for example to a call center or an emergency service, nothing in the signaling says which spoken, written or signed language they need, so the call may reach someone who cannot communicate with them.
tldr.mechanism: Two new media-level SDP attributes, 'hlang-send' and 'hlang-recv', carry language tags in the offer in order of preference, and the answer picks one language per direction.
tldr.outcome: Language is negotiated like any other property of a media stream, so a call can be handled by a suitable call taker or a translator or relay can be bridged in during setup. The RFC has since been updated by RFC 8865.

facts.label: Offer value
facts.value: One or more language tags, in preference order

today: RFC 8373 is a Proposed Standard that has been updated by RFC 8865. It defines the attributes and the offer and answer rules, and leaves user interface issues and language-based routing to other work.

sections.title: Why a Call Should Agree on a Language
sections.content:
A mutually comprehensible language is helpful for human communication. This document addresses the negotiation of human language and media modality, spoken, signed or written, in real-time communications. A companion document, RFC 8255, addresses language selection in email.

Unless the caller and callee know each other, or there is contextual or out-of-band information from which the languages and media modalities can be determined, the languages and modalities have to be negotiated from the caller's needs and the callee's capabilities. This applies to emergency and non-emergency calls alike. A non-emergency example is a caller contacting a company call center; an emergency call typically involves a caller contacting a Public Safety Answering Point (PSAP). In both cases it helps for the caller to indicate the preferred signed, written and spoken languages, and for the callee to indicate its capabilities, so that the call can proceed in the languages and media forms that both support.

The RFC uses the Session Description Protocol (SDP) for this, for various reasons, including the ability to establish multiple streams using different media such as voice, text and video. Treating language as another SDP attribute that is negotiated along with the other aspects of a media stream lets a range of user needs and called-party facilities be accommodated. Some users can speak several languages but have a preference. Some called parties support some of those languages internally but need a translation service for others, or have a limited number of call takers who can use certain languages. A user who can speak but is deaf or hard of hearing may want a voice stream to send spoken language plus a text stream to receive written language.
sections.plainLanguage: Two people who do not share a language cannot talk to each other. The signalling for a call has to carry the caller's language needs and the called party's language support, so that the call reaches someone who can understand. The same applies to sign language and to written language, and to emergency calls as much as to ordinary ones.

sections.title: What the Mechanism Should Do
sections.content:
The desired solution is a media attribute, preferably per direction, used in an offer to indicate the preferred languages of each direction of a media stream, and used in an answer to indicate the accepted language. When an offer carries several languages for a media stream, they are listed in order of preference, most preferred first.

Negotiating several simultaneous languages within one media stream is out of scope for this document.

In the offer and answer model used here, the offer contains a set of languages per media and direction that the offerer can use, and the answer contains one language per media and direction that the answerer will support. The answer states the media and languages that the answerer is committing to support, possibly after extra steps such as bridging an external translation or relay resource into the call, or having the call handled by an agent who speaks the requested language or can use the requested modality. Both sides therefore know what was negotiated. The extra steps needed to support an indicated language or modality may or may not be in place in time for any early media.
sections.plainLanguage: The offer lists every language the caller can use, in order of preference. The answer names exactly one language per direction and media stream, which is what the other side will actually use. Answering in a language may need extra work, such as bringing in a translator, and the answer is a statement of intent to support it.

sections.title: Why Not the Existing lang Attribute
sections.content:
RFC 4566 specifies a lang attribute that is similar to what is needed here, but it is not sufficiently specific or flexible for the needs of this document. The attribute is not mentioned in RFC 3264, and there are no known implementations in SIP. It is also useful to be able to specify a language per direction, for sending and for receiving.

This document therefore defines two new attributes, hlang-send and hlang-recv, both starting with hlang, short for human language.
sections.plainLanguage: SDP already has a lang attribute, but it does not say enough, it was never wired into the offer and answer model, and no one implemented it. It also cannot say one language for sending and another for receiving, so two new attributes are defined.

sections.title: The hlang-send and hlang-recv Attributes
sections.content:
Both attributes are media-level attributes and can appear in offers and answers. In an offer, the hlang-send value is a list of one or more languages the offerer is willing to use when sending with that media, and the hlang-recv value is a list of one or more languages the offerer is willing to use when receiving. The list is in preference order, first is most preferred. When a media is intended for interactive communication in only one direction, either attribute may be omitted, and the media can still be useful in both directions. When a media is not primarily intended for language, for example a video or audio stream for background only, both should be omitted. Otherwise both should have the same value. Specifying different languages for each direction can make the call difficult to complete, for example wanting to send audio in Hungarian and receive audio in Portuguese.

In an answer, hlang-send is the language the answerer will send if it uses the media for language, which in most cases is one of the languages in the offer's hlang-recv, and hlang-recv is the language the answerer expects to receive, which in most cases is one of the languages in the offer's hlang-send.

In an offer, each value must be a list of one or more language tags per BCP 47, separated by whitespace. In an answer, each value must be one language tag per BCP 47. BCP 47 describes the mechanisms for matching language tags, and Section 4.1 of RFC 5646 advises tagging content wisely and not including unnecessary subtags.

When an emergency call is placed, and in any other case where the language cannot be inferred from context, each offered media stream primarily intended for human language communication should specify the attributes for the directions intended for interactive communication. Clients acting for end users are expected to set one or both attributes on each offered media stream primarily intended for human communication when placing an outgoing session, and either to ignore or to take the attributes into account when receiving incoming calls, based on local configuration and capabilities. Systems acting for call centers and PSAPs are expected to take the attributes into account when processing inbound calls.
sections.plainLanguage: Each media stream carries its own language values, one for what is sent and one for what is received. In the offer the value is a list, most wanted first. In the answer it is a single tag. For a stream used in one direction only, the other attribute can be left out, and for a stream that carries no language at all, both should be left out.

sections.title: When There Is No Language in Common
sections.content:
The RFC does not mandate either behaviour for the case where the callee supports none of the languages the caller asked for. It is up to the implementation whether the call proceeds or fails.

When a call is rejected because there is no language in common, the SIP response has the response code 488 (Not Acceptable Here) or 606 (Not Acceptable), and a Warning header field with a warning code of 308. The warning text indicates that there are no mutually supported languages, and should also contain the supported languages and media. The RFC gives this example:

Warning:  308 proxy.example.com  "Incompatible language
   specification: Requested languages not supported.  Supported
   languages are: es, en; supported media are: audio, text."
sections.plainLanguage: The RFC leaves it open whether a call with no common language should go ahead or be refused. If it is refused, the refusal carries SIP code 488 or 606 and a warning that says which languages and media the other side does support, so the caller can try again.

sections.title: How a Language Tag Maps to a Media Stream
sections.content:
A sign-language tag with a video media stream is read as an indication of sign language in the video stream. A non-sign-language tag with a text media stream is read as an indication of written language in the text stream. A non-sign-language tag with an audio media stream is read as an indication of spoken language in the audio stream.

The RFC defines no other use for language tags in video media, such as how to indicate visible captions in the video stream, and it does not define the use of sign-language tags in text or audio media. It also does not define the use of language tags in media other than interactive streams of audio, video and text, such as message or application; that could be supported by later work or by agreement between the applications.

In the IANA registry for language subtags, a language subtag with a Type field of extlang combined with a Prefix field value of sgn indicates a sign-language tag. The absence of that sgn prefix indicates a non-sign-language tag.
sections.plainLanguage: The media stream says what kind of language it carries: video carries sign language, text carries written language and audio carries spoken language. A tag is a sign-language tag when it has the sgn prefix in the IANA language subtag registry.

sections.title: Worked Examples
sections.content:
The RFC gives several examples of the relevant SDP lines. Spoken English in both directions:

m=audio 49170 RTP/AVP 0
a=hlang-send:en
a=hlang-recv:en

American Sign Language in both directions:

m=video 51372 RTP/AVP 31 32
a=hlang-send:ase
a=hlang-recv:ase

An offer asking for spoken Spanish first, spoken Basque second and spoken English third:

m=audio 49250 RTP/AVP 20
a=hlang-send:es eu en
a=hlang-recv:es eu en

The answer picking Spanish in both directions:

m=audio 49250 RTP/AVP 20
a=hlang-send:es
a=hlang-recv:es

An alternative answer in which the callee supports none of the requested languages but chooses to proceed, using Italian:

m=audio 49250 RTP/AVP 20
a=hlang-send:it
a=hlang-recv:it

A richer offer asks for three streams: video for the caller to send using Argentine Sign Language, text for the caller to send using written Spanish or written Portuguese, and audio for the caller to receive spoken Spanish or spoken Portuguese.

m=video 51372 RTP/AVP 31 32
a=hlang-send:aed

m=text 45020 RTP/AVP 103 104
a=hlang-send:sp pt

m=audio 49250 RTP/AVP 20
a=hlang-recv:sp pt

The answer to that offer keeps the text and audio streams and declines the video, because the answering party has no video capability:

m=video 0 RTP/AVP 31 32
m=text 45020 RTP/AVP 103 104
a=hlang-recv:sp

m=audio 49250 RTP/AVP 20
a=hlang-send:sp

The RFC notes that even though the examples use the same language in both directions, that is not required, though in practice it makes a successful match more likely.
sections.plainLanguage: The examples show the same two attributes in use for a single language, for a preference list, and for a call that uses three media streams at once: video for sign language, text for writing and audio for speech. The answer can decline a stream it cannot support, by setting its port to zero.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The security considerations of BCP 47 apply here. An attacker able to modify the signalling could prevent a call from succeeding by altering crucial elements, including the hlang-send and hlang-recv values. RFC 5069 discusses such threats. The use of TLS or IPsec can protect against them.

Emergency calls are of particular concern. RFC 6881, which is specific to emergency calls, mandates the use of TLS or IPsec.
sections.plainLanguage: Changing the language values in the signalling can break a call, so the signalling has to be protected. TLS or IPsec do that, and emergency calls must use one of them.
